entities.name: Theuderic IV
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Theuderic IV, born in 712 CE, nominally held the title of Merovingian king of the Franks from 721 until his death in 737 CE, a period that profoundly reshaped the political landscape of Francia. As the last Merovingian monarch to reign for a significant duration before the interregnum, his tenure underscored the complete erosion of royal authority, with the actual governance and military power firmly concentrated in the hands of the Mayors of the Palace. His reign is historically significant not for his own actions, but as a crucial transitional phase demonstrating the irreversible decline of the Merovingian dynasty and the ascendance of the Carolingian house through the formidable figure of Charles Martel.

Ascending to the throne at the age of nine following the death of his father Dagobert III, Theuderic IV was entirely a puppet ruler, controlled first by Ragenfrid and then, more definitively, by Charles Martel. Martel, the powerful Mayor of the Palace, effectively governed the Frankish realm, conducting military campaigns against the Frisians, Saxons, and Bavarians, and crucially, repelling the Umayyad invasion at the Battle of Tours (Poitiers) in 732 CE. Theuderic's role was purely ceremonial; he issued no known edicts, led no armies, and exercised no independent political will, symbolizing the 'rois fainéants' (do-nothing kings) who merely lent a veneer of legitimacy to the burgeoning Carolingian power.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Theuderic IV's reign, though personally inconsequential, serves as a critical marker in the transfer of power from the Merovingian kings to the Carolingian Mayors of the Palace, directly preceding the six-year interregnum and the eventual Carolingian accession.
